# Legacy numbering in the reference application

Original OPC/XML fixture generated by `tools/legacy_numbering_fixture.py`. No
third-party engine or corpus content is included. The reference application
exported the reference on 2026-09-18 without saving the source. `reference.json`
records source/PDF hashes and label/text x coordinates in points for all 24 cases.
The PNG is a 96 DPI PDF render.

ECMA-376 Part 4 §14.6.2 specifies a default-on legacy flag, symbol indentation
from the text margin and spacing between symbol and text. The reference application differs:

- An omitted flag acts as off. Explicit on/1/true activates legacy placement.
- The ordinary first-line indent anchors the label area. `legacyIndent` gives
  its width; when absent, the hanging distance supplies that width. It does not
  place the symbol at the specified offset from the page text margin.
- For nonnegative widths, text follows the larger of that width and the measured
  label width plus `legacySpace`. The saved suffix adds no further tab/space.
  Left alignment starts at the ordinary first-line position; right alignment
  leaves the declared gap before text; center alignment centers in the declared
  width and clamps a too-short area to its start.
- Negative legacy indentation suppresses the visible label and moves first-line
  text by that signed distance. The numbering counter still exists.

Cases cover modern/off/omitted flags, zero/missing/negative values, short/large
gaps, three alignments, each suffix, different ordinary indents and no ordinary
indentation. Browser tests compare all 24 first-line coordinates with the reference application within
0.2 pt, allowing native font/PDF rounding. This is horizontal-placement evidence,
not complete line-height/font-metric equivalence with the native reference.

Unit tests cover retained package parts, text edits, restart, reopen, undo,
continuation indentation, measurement units and malformed declarations. Import
retains source numbering XML; generated definitions can serialize these
properties. New ordinary lists continue to use modern numbering.
